description: We are a team building SPHEREx AI Sky Explorer, a web-based tool that uses NASA SPHEREx data and AI to help discover and investigate changes in the sky over time.
summary: NASA's SPHEREx telescope photographs the entire sky every six months, but its pictures sit in a scientific archive that only experts know how to use. ARCNAVE opens that archive to everyone. Type any place in the sky, or a star's name, and ARCNAVE plays NASA's real SPHEREx pictures of that spot like a short video, so anything that moves or changes stands out, just as Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto in 1930 by flipping between two photographs. Every moving star is circled, measured, and checked against ESA's Gaia map of the stars. We tested ARCNAVE on all five stars NASA chose for this challenge, and it caught every one: Barnard's Star, for example, moved 9.9 arcseconds in a year, where astronomers expect 10.2. ARCNAVE runs on any phone and needs no sign-in, so a student, a teacher or a curious stargazer can watch the real sky change, and perhaps spot the next moving world.
details:
What it does

  1. Pick a spot. Type a sky position (RA and Dec) or a name such as "Barnard's Star".
  2. Watch it change. NASA's real pictures of that spot play in date order, like a little video. You can also blink between two dates, or subtract one from the other to see only what changed.
  3. See what moved. Every moving star is circled in each picture, its speed is measured, and the result is compared with known star catalogues. Every result says how sure we are.

How it answers the challenge

  • Enter the RA and Dec of a patch of sky: type a position or a name, or click the map of the whole sky.
  • Show the pictures like a little video: play as a video, step by step, blink or swipe.
  • Make moving objects easy to spot: movers circled in every picture, with their path.
  • Test on the five named stars: all five measured and compared with known values.
  • Easy to update with new data releases: NASA's newest release (November 2026) appeared with no change to our code.

We also built every extra idea the challenge suggested: SPHEREx's 102 colours and the spectrum of any star, adding and subtracting pictures, choosing the field of view, Gaia and WISE star maps on top, links that open any spot, NASA's data-quality flags, and export to Python and Aladin.

NASA's five test stars

  • Barnard's Star, the fastest-moving star in our sky: moved 9.9" a year (expected 10.2").
  • Epsilon Indi B, a pair of brown dwarfs near the Sun: moved 4.3" a year (expected 4.7").
  • WISE 0855, the coldest brown dwarf known: moved 8.8" a year; agrees with NASA WISE.
  • RW Aurigae, a young star that dims: became about half as bright in a year.
  • R Draconis, a pulsating giant star: its brightness changed about three times over.

Why you can trust it

Before trusting ARCNAVE, we tried to fool it. We hid 19,880 fake planets in real SPHEREx pictures across 18 parts of the sky, picked before we started. A planet as far as 1,000 times Earth's distance from the Sun was found in all 18. Where it misses, we show the miss. Nothing is ever called a discovery.

Why it matters

  • Students and the public: real space data as a video, on a phone, with a 60-second "Find the asteroid" game and a 90-second story.
  • Citizen scientists: a free tool to look for nearby brown dwarfs and distant moving objects, with the usual checks done for them.
  • Scientists: real measurements with error bars, and a Python notebook to repeat them.
  • NASA: every new SPHEREx release is ready for the public on the day it comes out.

What's next

Re-measure every result on SPHEREx's newest release, and add a volunteer mode where many people check the same patch of sky together.

Built with

JavaScript in the browser, a small Node.js server with no add-ons, the Aladin Lite sky viewer, Python and Astropy for the notebook export, and Cloudflare hosting. ARCNAVE reads only the part of each picture it needs (about 4 MB instead of 65 MB), so it stays quick even on a phone.
